coherence.reasons: X runs one logical chain from governing thought to slides: is it worth launching (sized at $1.2–2.9M), how to package it (Pro with an allowance), when (after mobile), and what would change the answer. Slide 3 tests the CPO's plan against five conditions, and each verdict maps to a later slide. It has minor tensions: 14% is called a ceiling for the add-on but used as the low case for Pro, and slide 13 says the sequence matters less than delivering both. Y's four sections are clean and its titles match its evidence. But its logic strains at the key point: it calls the mobile delay the launch's biggest risk, with 4.5 times the churn, and still launches in Q2. The only bridge is one line, that $1.1M at risk is below the $2.9M Pro adds, plus a Q3 gate that fires after the delay has already happened. Y also discounts the 14% paywall figure as a ceiling while planning on a single 33% precedent as its point estimate.

judgment.reasons: Both reach defensible conclusions under the key: Y is R1 (Pro tier with a cap, delay accepted explicitly) and X is R3 with a Pro design. X meets the R3 conditions: it quantifies the win-rate risk (at most $0.64M a year) and plans a limited AI response (paid early access for beta plus about 250 random accounts, positioned as 'AI included in Pro'). X weighs the central trade-off much better. It compares two-quarter delay costs on both sides ($0.5–1.1M for mobile against at most $0.56M for Copilot), gives a break-even (the rewrite must fix 26–52% of mobile churn), and names triggers that would flip the timing, including the Q4 win rate and whether the 14 engineers can come from outside mobile. Its weakness is that the Copilot revenue deferral ($0.1–0.7M of gross profit) sits outside the headline comparison, which makes the timing call closer than the title suggests. Y accepts the delay on a thin comparison of one-off churn risk against annual Pro ARR that is deferred rather than lost. Its gate cannot undo the delay, and its allowance of about 850 requests per seat is set exactly at the 75% floor, with no headroom. Y considers three packaging options but no timing alternative.

evidence.reasons: Both get the required numbers right: $8.06M against $2.45M, inference of $32.4 / $61.2 / $130.5 a month, about 109 deals and $0.64M, and $2.89M for Pro. Both handle the VP Sales claim, the Routewise promo, beta selection bias and the survey's 6% response rate. X goes further on the critical evidence. It shows the VP claim implies a 58% win rate, stress-tests company margin with heavy-user upgraders (74.1% without a cap, 75.9% with), gives feature margins with and without platform cost, builds an NRR bridge, and grades how far each beta measure can be trusted. Its invented parameters (7% haircut, 600-request allowance, $20 top-up, 50% of mobile churn fixed) are labelled as illustrative and listed in an appendix. Y's arithmetic is sound, including the 5,297-request breakeven, 70% margin for free-in-Core and 17-month payback. But it plans on 33% Pro uptake from a single 2023 precedent with no low case. It never states Pro's own margin. Its slide 4 title ('Copilot delivers in daily use') runs ahead of volunteer data, though the body caveats it.

revision.reasons: Both revise the CPO's hypothesis as the key expects: keep the launch, reject the $149 add-on and the $8M figure, and explain the gap between 46% stated and 14% revealed demand along with the survey's biases. X does this more explicitly and with more discipline. It breaks the hypothesis into five testable conditions with verdicts, resets the case to a range of $1.2–2.9M, and revises the timing with the mobile trade-off argued in numbers, which the key allows. Y revises packaging and sizing correctly, but swaps the survey point estimate for another largely untested one ($2.9M at 33%) with no downside case. It keeps the Q2 timing without really testing it against the mobile evidence it cites.

overall.reasons: Both avoid every trap and recommend a Pro tier with usage guardrails, so either would steer the CEO away from the $149 add-on and the $8M forecast. X serves the decision better. It gives a range rather than a point estimate, a margin stress test with a cap that leaves headroom, and a quantified two-sided timing comparison with break-evens. It also names decision triggers readable at January planning (the Q4 win rate and engineer sourcing) that would move the launch back to Q2. Y is tighter and its accepted-delay answer is defensible. But its justification for accepting the top churn driver's delay is thin, its gate is weak, and its plan rests on a single 33% precedent. X's main flaw is that its timing margin is narrower than presented once the revenue deferral is counted, but it says so and attaches triggers.
